output.query: seizure versus syncope differentiation convulsive syncope older adults

results.summary: Seizure and syncope share superficial features including loss of consciousness and convulsive movements. Key discriminators: postictal confusion > 5 minutes favors seizure (sensitivity 70%, specificity 85%); stereotyped aura (epigastric rising, deja vu, fear) with subsequent impaired awareness strongly suggests temporal lobe seizure; convulsive syncope involves brief (<15 s) tonic or myoclonic activity during cerebral hypoperfusion without a preceding aura. Witnessed oroalimentary automatisms are highly specific for temporal lobe seizures. Prolonged post-event confusion is not seen in syncope.
results.title: Clinical differentiation of seizures and syncope

results.summary: A prolactin level drawn 10-20 minutes after a witnessed tonic-clonic or focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure that is at least twice the baseline level or above the laboratory upper limit of normal supports a diagnosis of epileptic seizure over syncope. Sensitivity approximately 60% for generalized tonic-clonic seizures; lower sensitivity for focal seizures. Normal prolactin does not exclude epilepsy. Tilt-table-induced syncope typically does not produce significant prolactin elevation.
results.title: Post-ictal prolactin as a biomarker to distinguish epileptic seizures from syncope

results.summary: New-onset temporal lobe epilepsy in adults over age 50 most commonly results from remote structural injury (post-traumatic, vascular, remote herpes simplex encephalitis), hippocampal sclerosis (with or without early febrile-seizure history), or small low-grade lesions. The initial presentation is frequently delayed diagnosis of 2-4 years due to misattribution to syncope, TIA, or anxiety. Epigastric aura and deja vu are the most prevalent aura types in this age group.
results.title: Temporal lobe epilepsy in adults over age 50: clinical features and etiology

output.summary: Seizure-syncope differentiation rests on several clinical discriminators. Stereotyped aura (epigastric rising, deja vu), post-event confusion exceeding 5 minutes, and witnessed oroalimentary automatisms point strongly to temporal lobe seizure. Brief (<15 s) convulsive movements without aura favor convulsive syncope. Elevated post-ictal prolactin (at least doubling, drawn 10-20 minutes post-event) supports an epileptic seizure but is not diagnostic alone and has limited sensitivity for focal events. A negative tilt-table and Holter in the context of stereotyped temporal-lobe semiology substantially reduces the probability of vasovagal or cardiogenic syncope. Temporal lobe epilepsy is a leading cause of delayed or misdiagnosed paroxysmal events in adults over 50, particularly when convulsive features are present.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the events to cardiac syncope when all cardiac investigations are negative and EEG demonstrates epileptiform activity concordant with the clinical semiology.
Do not implant a pacemaker or cardiac event recorder for management of these events when EEG confirms epileptic etiology.
Do not prescribe flecainide, sotalol, or other antiarrhythmic agents for these events.
Do not escalate cardiac interventions (electrophysiology study, ablation) in the absence of a documented cardiac arrhythmia.
Do not initiate carbamazepine or phenytoin in a patient taking atorvastatin without acknowledging the CYP3A4 interaction that substantially reduces statin exposure.
required_recommendations: Capture habitual events with video-EEG to confirm epileptic etiology and localize seizure onset to the right temporal region.

Recognize that stereotyped epigastric aura, deja vu, oroalimentary automatisms, and post-ictal confusion exceeding 5 minutes are semiology inconsistent with syncope and characteristic of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
Recognize elevated post-ictal prolactin (drawn 22 minutes post-event) as supporting an epileptic seizure over syncopal event.

Initiate appropriate first-line AED for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam or lacosamide preferred given drug interaction profile with existing medications); avoid enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin) that reduce atorvastatin levels.
Counsel patient on driving restrictions per applicable local regulations until seizure-free interval is achieved on treatment.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup with a structural etiology on MRI.
CT is inferior to epilepsy-protocol MRI for detecting hippocampal sclerosis and remote cortical lesions; adds ionizing radiation without incremental diagnostic value when dedicated MRI is available.
FDG-PET is reserved for surgical evaluation in MRI-negative refractory epilepsy; not indicated at first diagnosis when MRI clearly localizes the lesion and EEG is concordant.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin (focal-onset seizures with impaired awareness and secondary focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic evolution), with right mesial temporal sclerosis and remote cortical injury

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive movements + blackouts in a 55-year-old man with cardiac family history warranted cardiac workup; extensive cardiac evaluation was negative (normal Holter, negative tilt-table, no arrhythmia, normal EF on echo).
Common in middle-aged adults; excluded by negative head-up tilt-table test and absence of postural or emotional triggers.
Episodic behavioral events in middle age; excluded by video-EEG capture of habitual events with electrographic right temporal ictal correlate.

differential.diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) of posterior circulation
differential.key_features: Age, hypertension, and paroxysmal neurological symptoms raise vascular concern; however, TIAs produce negative phenomena (weakness, sensory loss), not aura with automatisms, and do not cause post-event confusion of this duration.
Frontal seizures may include motor features; epigastric aura, deja vu, oroalimentary automatisms, and EEG/MRI concordance with right temporal structures argue against frontal origin.

key_clinical_evidence: The syncope hypothesis is clinically reasonable given convulsive movements, blackouts, and a cardiac family history — making the cardiac workup justified, not a misuse of resources. The key pivot is recognizing that all cardiac tests were negative while the clinical semiology (epigastric aura, deja vu, oroalimentary automatisms, post-ictal confusion > 5 minutes) is characteristic of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.

Post-ictal prolactin elevation (48 ng/mL, drawn 22 minutes after a witnessed convulsive episode) is a supportive biomarker for an epileptic convulsion rather than syncope; syncope does not consistently elevate prolactin.

EEG laterality and MRI laterality must agree: right anterior temporal sharp-and-slow-wave discharges with phase reversal at F8 are concordant with right hippocampal sclerosis and right temporal pole remote lesion on MRI.

Convulsive syncope involves brief (<15 seconds) tonic-clonic movements during cerebral hypoperfusion without a preceding aura, and does not produce post-event confusion lasting minutes; the 5-minute post-ictal confusion and stereotyped epigastric-deja vu aura in this case are incompatible with syncope.

Older-onset temporal lobe epilepsy (over age 50) frequently results from remote structural injury or mesial temporal sclerosis and is commonly misdiagnosed as syncope or TIA for years before the correct diagnosis is established.

Carbamazepine and phenytoin should be avoided given CYP3A4 induction effects on atorvastatin; levetiracetam or lacosamide are preferred first-line options for focal epilepsy with no significant interactions in this drug regimen.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Laboratory testing does not diagnose focal epilepsy; it addresses a provoked seizure or a metabolic mimic when one is suspected.

July 2026 review applied end to end: routine EEG first when appropriate, staged sleep-deprived/ambulatory escalation, video only for event capture or tertiary evaluation, and continuous ICU EEG only for NCSE.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Brief convulsive activity can occur as a secondary feature of temporal lobe seizures with bilateral tonic-clonic evolution; convulsive syncope lacks a stereotyped aura and produces no post-event confusion beyond seconds. The semiology here (epigastric aura + deja vu preceding loss of awareness + prolonged post-ictal confusion) is incompatible with syncope.
red_herrings.data_point: Witnessed brief convulsive movements during one blackout episode, attributed by the emergency department to convulsive syncope.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on the convulsive movements and cardiac family history as evidence of cardiogenic syncope; extend and repeat cardiac workup rather than pursuing neurological evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A PR interval of 194 ms is at the borderline of the upper normal limit (200 ms) and does not constitute a high-grade conduction abnormality. This isolated finding is not a cardiac cause of recurrent blackouts. The full cardiac evaluation (Holter, tilt-table, echocardiogram) was collectively negative.
red_herrings.data_point: Borderline first-degree AV block on 12-lead ECG (PR interval 194 ms).
red_herrings.intended_effect: Over-interpret a borderline ECG finding as a potential cardiac cause warranting electrophysiology referral or additional cardiac workup, delaying neurological evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Negative cardiac workup is necessary to exclude syncope when the differential is genuinely open, but it does not establish an alternative diagnosis. The presence of stereotyped temporal-lobe semiology demands EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI regardless of cardiac workup completeness.
red_herrings.data_point: Extensive 8-week prior cardiac workup (ECG, 48-hour Holter, echocardiogram, tilt-table) performed before neurology referral.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Assume that because cardiology completed a thorough workup, a cardiac cause has been excluded and the diagnosis is idiopathic/functional; overlook the epileptic semiology and delay EEG evaluation.

metadata.difficulty_description: Older-onset mesial temporal lobe epilepsy initially misdiagnosed as convulsive/cardiac syncope. The puzzle requires recognizing that the negative cardiac workup (ECG, Holter, echo, tilt-table) was clinically justified given genuine syncope-vs-seizure differential, but its negativity combined with epileptiform EEG and concordant MRI confirms the epileptic diagnosis. Key discriminators include semiology (epigastric aura, deja vu, oroalimentary automatisms, 5-minute post-ictal confusion) and elevated post-ictal prolactin. Tests cardiac tools in the justified-not-useless slot — appropriate for this specific differential.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Seven optimal tools (6 required, 3 recommended), three embedded red herrings, requires synthesis across cardiac and neurological modalities to correctly classify the epileptic vs. syncope differential. Cardiac tools (ECG, Holter, echo, tilt-table) are justified by genuine syncope differential and classified recommended-not-useless for this case.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. H is a 55-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a remote closed head injury at age 38, who presents for inpatient neurology evaluation following a 6-month history of recurrent paroxysmal episodes that were initially attributed to vasovagal or cardiac syncope. The episodes began insidiously approximately 6 months ago. They are stereotyped: the patient first notices a vague uncomfortable rising sensation from the epigastrium toward the chest, followed by an intense, brief feeling of deja vu ('I know I've been here before but I know I haven't'). He then loses awareness of his surroundings. His wife, who has witnessed multiple episodes, reports that he stares blankly, makes chewing and lip-smacking movements, and occasionally performs repetitive fumbling motions with his right hand. Episodes last 60-90 seconds on average. Post-ictally, he is confused and fatigued for approximately 5 minutes before returning to full alertness. He reports having no memory of the episode itself.

Approximately 3 months ago, one episode was witnessed by his wife and involved brief slumping with approximately 15-20 seconds of rhythmic right arm jerking before he regained consciousness. This episode prompted urgent cardiac evaluation, as his father died of a myocardial infarction, and the convulsive movements were initially interpreted by the emergency department as consistent with convulsive syncope. Extensive cardiac workup over the following 8 weeks included a 12-lead ECG (borderline findings, see below), a 48-hour Holter monitor (no arrhythmia), a transthoracic echocardiogram (normal), and a head-up tilt-table test (negative for vasovagal response). All cardiac studies were unrevealing, and cardiology referred him for neurological evaluation. He has had a total of 11 episodes over 6 months. No clear positional or exertional trigger for any episode. No prodromal lightheadedness, diaphoresis, or pallor reported before the deja vu aura. He has self-restricted driving since the second episode. He has not been started on any antiepileptic medication.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue lacerations. No urinary incontinence reported with episodes. Patient reports one episode in which he briefly lost postural tone and slumped in a chair, which was witnessed by his wife who called emergency services. That episode involved brief rhythmic jerking of the right arm for approximately 15-20 seconds before the convulsive movements stopped.
